newsitem.title: HONG KONG: S&P assigns "A" rating to Pacific Palisades debt.
newsitem.headline: S&P assigns "A" rating to Pacific Palisades debt.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Thursday it assigned its "A" long-term credit rating to debt securities issued by Pacific Palisades Funding Ltd, comprising US$98.8 million floating rate notes and 22.5 million stg fixed rate notes.
Palisades is ultimately owned 20 percent by Sino Land Co Ltd and 80 percent by the Ng family, who are the majority shareholders in Sino Land, S&P said.
Both tranches of debt are secured and due November 2001.

The notes are secured by the Pacific Palisades apartment complex, a 425-unit, high-rise residential property in Hong Kong. Rental revenue generated from Pacific Palisades is the source of the scheduled interest payment on the notes.
The transaction marked the second, single-property commercial real estate securitisation in Hong Kong to be assigned a rating by S&P, the rating agency said.
It said the single-A rating reflected the strong debt service coverage ratio of 1.9 times and the intitial 31.4 percent loan-to-value ratio.
It took into account an initial reserve fund and additional retention of surplus cash flows in the reserve fund should the debt service coverage ratio deteriorate.
It also took into consideration a swap agreement provided by Bankers Trust Co, Hong Kong branch, to cover interest rate and currency risks.
The rating also reflected good overall credit quality of the tenants and property, and sound mechanics and legal structure of the transaction and comprehensive insurance policies.
Rating factors include the volatility of Hong Kong property market and Japanese expatriate tenant concentration.
This is mitigated by the property's location in a market with favourable supply and demand fundamentals.

The sustainability of current market rental levels and occupancy rates were considered against the rating agency's benchmarks for this type of financing, and adjusted for the particular historical experience and risks of the Hong Kong environment, Standard & Poor's said.
